Paper I - Financial Accounting (50 Marks)

Accounting & Auditing · Group 1 · 2,504 words · about 13 min read

 On this page

A. The Ideas Behind the Rules (Accounting Concepts and Qualities)
B. The Accounting Equation and Double Entry
C. The Recording Cycle: Journal to Ledger to Trial Balance
D. Period-End Adjustments
E. The Four Financial Statements, and How They Connect
F. Who Reads This, and Why It Matters
G. Accounting for Different Forms of Organization
H. Non-Current Tangible Assets and Depreciation
I. Reading the Statements: Financial-Statement Analysis

Test paragraph only.

Treat this paper as one continuous story rather than 29 separate facts. A transaction happens; it is recorded through double entry; entries are grouped into ledger accounts; the ledger is checked through a trial balance; end-of-period adjustments correct timing issues; the corrected figures become four connected statements; and those statements are then read and compared through ratios. Everything below sits somewhere on that line.

A. The Ideas Behind the Rules (Accounting Concepts and Qualities)

Before any numbers, accounting rests on a small set of assumptions and qualities. Each one exists to stop financial statements from becoming misleading, and each shows up later as a reason why a specific rule works the way it does.

Accrual and matching: Income is recorded when it is earned, and expenses when they are incurred, not simply when cash changes hands. Matching then ties an expense to the period whose revenue it helped generate. Why it matters: without accrual accounting, a firm that delays paying its bills would look artificially profitable, and one that pays early would look artificially poor. Example: electricity used in June but paid in July is still June’s expense, because the use happened in June.
Consistency and comparability: The same accounting method should be used period after period unless there is a genuine, disclosed reason to change. This is what makes a trend meaningful rather than an artifact of switching methods.
True and fair presentation: The overall objective that statements should faithfully represent the entity’s actual financial reality, not just satisfy a checklist.
Neutrality, materiality, prudence, completeness, understandability: These are the qualities that make information useful. Neutral means not deliberately slanted. Material means important enough that its omission could change a user’s decision, and materiality is relative to the size of the entity. Prudence means exercising care under uncertainty; it is not permission to deliberately understate profit or assets. Completeness means nothing relevant has been left out. Understandability means a reasonably informed reader can follow the report.
Going concern and substance over form: Going concern assumes the business will keep operating for the foreseeable future, which justifies carrying assets at cost rather than forced-sale value. Substance over form means the economic reality of a transaction governs its accounting treatment, even if its legal label suggests otherwise.

Key takeaway: every one of these concepts answers the same question: what would make this information misleading, and how do we stop that? Learn them that way rather than as unconnected vocabulary.

B. The Accounting Equation and Double Entry

The entire system rests on one identity that must hold after every single transaction: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

Double entry is the mechanism that keeps this equation balanced: every transaction is recorded as at least one debit and one equal credit. A common beginner error is treating “debit” as meaning “increase” in general; it depends entirely on the account type:

Assets and expenses normally increase with a debit and decrease with a credit.
Liabilities, equity and income normally increase with a credit and decrease with a debit.

Worked example: the owner invests Rs 100,000 cash into the business. Cash (an asset) increases, so it is debited Rs 100,000. Capital (equity) increases, so it is credited Rs 100,000. The equation still balances.

The practical skill here is not memorizing rules but being able to ask, for any transaction: which two (or more) accounts changed, and in which direction? Working through many small transactions by hand, at least 30 as a starting target, is what turns this from a rule you look up into a reflex.

C. The Recording Cycle: Journal to Ledger to Trial Balance
General journal. Transactions are first recorded chronologically with a debit line, a credit line, and a short narration explaining what occurred. Example: a credit sale of Rs 20,000 is recorded as Debit Accounts Receivable 20,000, Credit Sales 20,000, because the business now has a right to collect cash later and has earned revenue now.
General ledger. The journal tells you what happened and when; the ledger reorganizes that same information by account, so you can ask what the balance of Cash is right now and get a single answer.
Trial balance. This lists every ledger account’s closing balance in two columns and checks that total debits equal total credits. It is a mechanical check, not a proof of correctness: some errors, such as omitting a transaction entirely, leave the trial balance perfectly balanced while the records are still wrong.
D. Period-End Adjustments
Before final statements can be prepared, the trial balance is adjusted to reflect the accrual concept properly. The four classic adjustments are:
Accrued expense: incurred but not yet paid or recorded, such as wages earned by staff in the last week of the period but paid next month.
Prepaid expense: paid in advance but not yet used up. A 12-month insurance premium of Rs 12,000 paid at the start of the year means that after 3 months, Rs 3,000 has been used and is an expense, and Rs 9,000 remains an asset called prepaid insurance.
Accrued income: earned but not yet received or recorded.
Unearned income: cash received, but the service or goods have not yet been delivered, so it is a liability until earned.
Once these are posted, an adjusted trial balance is produced, and this, not the original trial balance, is what final statements are built from.
A worksheet is an internal working paper used to organize the unadjusted balances, the adjustments, and the resulting adjusted figures side by side before the statements are typed up; it is a working tool, not a reported statement. Closing entries then transfer all temporary accounts, meaning revenue and expense accounts, into equity, because these accounts must start each new period at zero; permanent accounts simply carry their balances forward. Reversing entries, used optionally at the start of the next period, are a bookkeeping convenience that simplifies handling certain accruals.
Key takeaway (Sections B to D): the whole cycle is transaction, then journal, then ledger, then trial balance, then adjustments, then adjusted trial balance, then statements, then closing entries, then post-closing trial balance. If any stage feels abstract, carry one small transaction through the entire sequence by hand rather than memorizing each stage separately.
E. The Four Financial Statements, and How They Connect
A common mistake is treating profit, cash, and financial position as if they were the same thing. They are not, and each statement answers a different question.
Income statement: did we make a profit or loss over the period? Revenue minus expenses equals profit or loss. Example: revenue 500,000 minus expenses 420,000 gives profit 80,000.
Statement of financial position (balance sheet): what do we own and owe right now, at a single date? It lists assets (resources the entity controls), liabilities (present obligations it owes), and equity (the residual claim left after liabilities are deducted from assets), usually split into current and non-current items. Cash is normally current; a building used in operations is normally non-current.
Statement of cash flows: where did our cash actually come from and go, over the period? It explains cash movement under three headings: operating (day-to-day trading), investing (buying or selling long-term assets), and financing (borrowing, repaying, or raising capital). A firm can be profitable on paper while cash is tight, for example because customers haven’t paid yet, which is exactly why this statement exists alongside the income statement.
Statement of changes in equity: why did owners’ equity change over the period? It reconciles opening equity to closing equity by adding profit and any new owner contributions, and subtracting dividends or drawings and losses. Example: opening equity 1,000,000 plus profit 200,000 minus dividends 80,000 equals closing equity 1,120,000. This closing figure must always agree with the equity section of the statement of financial position, which is a good way to catch errors.
The connection to hold onto: profit from the income statement flows into equity via the statement of changes in equity, and the resulting equity balance appears on the statement of financial position, while the statement of cash flows tracks something related but genuinely different: cash movement, not profit.
F. Who Reads This, and Why It Matters
Different users read the same statements looking for different things.
External users: investors and shareholders look mainly at profitability and growth; lenders and banks look mainly at repayment capacity and cash flow; suppliers look mainly at short-term liquidity, meaning whether they will be paid on time; government and regulators look mainly at compliance and tax.
Internal users: directors and managers care about efficiency and decision-making; employees care about job security and stability.
A useful exam technique: build a user-to-information-need table for any organizational-form question, because it converts a vague theory prompt into a structured, markable answer.
G. Accounting for Different Forms of Organization
The accounting mechanics, meaning double entry, adjustments, and statements, stay the same across organizational forms. What changes is mainly the equity section and the reporting emphasis, because the legal form changes who owns the entity and who is accountable to whom.
Sole proprietorship: one owner. Equity tracks capital, additional investment, profit or loss, and drawings. Drawings, meaning cash or goods the owner takes for personal use, reduce equity directly; they are not a business expense, because they are not incurred to earn revenue.
Partnership: two or more partners under an agreement. Each partner has a capital or current account, and profit or loss is split according to the agreed profit-sharing ratio, plus interest on capital or drawings or partner salary if the agreement provides for these. Example: partners A and B share profit 3 to 2; a distributable profit of Rs 100,000 splits into Rs 60,000 and Rs 40,000 before any other agreement-specific adjustments. The agreement, not a default assumption, governs every distribution detail.
Joint-stock company: a separate legal entity from its owners, with share capital, reserves, retained earnings, and a more formal reporting structure. Issuing shares for cash increases both cash and share capital. At this syllabus level, advanced company-accounting topics such as amalgamation, capital reduction, and consolidation of group accounts are explicitly outside scope.
Banking companies: a fundamentally different business model. Banks accept deposits, which are a major liability since the bank owes this money back to depositors, and extend financing, which is an asset, so their statements reflect a liquidity- and risk-driven structure rather than a typical trading firm’s inventory-and-sales structure.
Not-for-profit associations: formed to pursue a purpose, not to distribute profit. Their statements often use receipts-and-payments, a cash basis, or income-and-expenditure, an accrual basis, depending on what is required. Example: a membership subscription can count as income of the period it relates to even if the cash arrives at a different time, once accrual logic is applied.
Public-sector accounting: the accountability question shifts from did we earn a profit, to was public money used lawfully, transparently, and for its intended service purpose. The FPSC syllabus points toward the IPSAS-oriented framework used in Pakistan’s public sector as the reference point for this stewardship-centered reporting.
Key takeaway (Sections F and G): for any accounting-for-organizational-form question, first ask who is accountable to whom, and for what purpose does this entity exist. The accounting treatment follows from that, not the other way around.
H. Non-Current Tangible Assets and Depreciation
Non-current tangible assets are physical resources used for more than one accounting period, such as buildings or machinery. Key vocabulary: cost is what was paid to acquire and prepare the asset for use; residual value is the expected value at the end of useful life; depreciable amount is cost minus residual value, the amount that will be spread over the asset’s life; useful life is the period over which the asset is expected to be used.
A critical point: depreciation is an allocation of cost over time, not a cash payment. No money leaves the business when depreciation is recorded; it simply spreads an already-incurred cost across the periods that benefit from using the asset, matching expense to the revenue the asset helps generate.
Three common methods, using a machine costing Rs 500,000, with residual value Rs 50,000 and useful life 5 years, giving a depreciable amount of Rs 450,000:
Straight-line: depreciable amount divided by useful life, so 450,000 divided by 5 equals Rs 90,000 per year, every year, assuming assumptions don’t change. Simple and appropriate when the asset is used roughly evenly over time.
Reducing-balance: a fixed percentage is applied each year to the asset’s remaining book value, not the original cost, so depreciation is highest in early years and falls over time. This suits assets that lose most of their usefulness early, such as some vehicles and technology.
Units-of-production: depreciation is tied to actual usage, such as machine-hours or units produced, rather than time, so it varies with how intensively the asset is used in a given period. Most appropriate when wear is driven by use rather than the passage of time.
Choosing the wrong method distorts profit trends and asset values on the statement of financial position, which is exactly why the consistency concept from Section A applies directly here: switching depreciation methods without disclosure would make one year’s profit incomparable to another’s for reasons that have nothing to do with real performance.
I. Reading the Statements: Financial-Statement Analysis
Once statements exist, they need to be read, not just prepared.
Horizontal analysis, also called trend analysis, compares the same line item across multiple periods, such as sales in Year 1 versus Year 2 versus Year 3, to spot growth, decline, or volatility over time.
Vertical analysis expresses each line item as a percentage of a base figure within the same period, such as each expense as a percentage of sales. Ratio analysis goes further by relating two figures to each other: profitability ratios such as net profit margin, liquidity ratios such as the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), and solvency ratios such as debt-to-equity.
The consistency concept matters again here: ratios and trends are only meaningful if the underlying accounting methods haven’t silently changed between the periods being compared. Technical and industry analysis goes one step further by placing a company’s ratios in the context of its specific industry’s norms, since a good current ratio for a retailer and for a heavy manufacturer can look very different.
Paper I (Financial Accounting) key takeaways: the whole paper is one connected cycle, from transaction to journal to ledger to trial balance to adjustments to the four statements to closing entries to ratio analysis. Every foundational concept, such as accrual, matching, consistency, prudence, going concern, and substance over form, exists to prevent a specific kind of misleading information; learn the reason, not just the label. Double-entry direction depends on account type, not a universal rule. A balanced trial balance is a necessary but not sufficient check. Depreciation reallocates cost over time and is never a cash outflow. The organizational form mainly changes the equity treatment and the accountability lens, not the underlying mechanics. Ratios and trends are only trustworthy when accounting methods have been applied consistently across the periods being compared.

Trial balance. This lists every ledger account’s closing balance in two columns and checks that total debits equal total credits. It is a mechanical check, not a proof of correctness: some errors, such as omitting a transaction entirely, leave the trial balance perfectly balanced while the records are still wrong.
D. Period-End Adjustments
Before final statements can be prepared, the trial balance is adjusted to reflect the accrual concept properly. The four classic adjustments are:
Accrued expense: incurred but not yet paid or recorded, such as wages earned by staff in the last week of the period but paid next month.
Prepaid expense: paid in advance but not yet used up. A 12-month insurance premium of Rs 12,000 paid at the start of the year means that after 3 months, Rs 3,000 has been used and is an expense, and Rs 9,000 remains an asset called prepaid insurance.
Accrued income: earned but not yet received or recorded.
Unearned income: cash received, but the service or goods have not yet been delivered, so it is a liability until earned.
Once these are posted, an adjusted trial balance is produced, and this, not the original trial balance, is what final statements are built from.
A worksheet is an internal working paper used to organize the unadjusted balances, the adjustments, and the resulting adjusted figures side by side before the statements are typed up; it is a working tool, not a reported statement. Closing entries then transfer all temporary accounts, meaning revenue and expense accounts, into equity, because these accounts must start each new period at zero; permanent accounts simply carry their balances forward. Reversing entries, used optionally at the start of the next period, are a bookkeeping convenience that simplifies handling certain accruals.
Key takeaway (Sections B to D): the whole cycle is transaction, then journal, then ledger, then trial balance, then adjustments, then adjusted trial balance, then statements, then closing entries, then post-closing trial balance. If any stage feels abstract, carry one small transaction through the entire sequence by hand rather than memorizing each stage separately.
E. The Four Financial Statements, and How They Connect
A common mistake is treating profit, cash, and financial position as if they were the same thing. They are not, and each statement answers a different question.
Income statement: did we make a profit or loss over the period? Revenue minus expenses equals profit or loss. Example: revenue 500,000 minus expenses 420,000 gives profit 80,000.
Statement of financial position (balance sheet): what do we own and owe right now, at a single date? It lists assets (resources the entity controls), liabilities (present obligations it owes), and equity (the residual claim left after liabilities are deducted from assets), usually split into current and non-current items. Cash is normally current; a building used in operations is normally non-current.
Statement of cash flows: where did our cash actually come from and go, over the period? It explains cash movement under three headings: operating (day-to-day trading), investing (buying or selling long-term assets), and financing (borrowing, repaying, or raising capital). A firm can be profitable on paper while cash is tight, for example because customers haven’t paid yet, which is exactly why this statement exists alongside the income statement.
Statement of changes in equity: why did owners’ equity change over the period? It reconciles opening equity to closing equity by adding profit and any new owner contributions, and subtracting dividends or drawings and losses. Example: opening equity 1,000,000 plus profit 200,000 minus dividends 80,000 equals closing equity 1,120,000. This closing figure must always agree with the equity section of the statement of financial position, which is a good way to catch errors.
The connection to hold onto: profit from the income statement flows into equity via the statement of changes in equity, and the resulting equity balance appears on the statement of financial position, while the statement of cash flows tracks something related but genuinely different: cash movement, not profit.
F. Who Reads This, and Why It Matters
Different users read the same statements looking for different things.
External users: investors and shareholders look mainly at profitability and growth; lenders and banks look mainly at repayment capacity and cash flow; suppliers look mainly at short-term liquidity, meaning whether they will be paid on time; government and regulators look mainly at compliance and tax.
Internal users: directors and managers care about efficiency and decision-making; employees care about job security and stability.
A useful exam technique: build a user-to-information-need table for any organizational-form question, because it converts a vague theory prompt into a structured, markable answer.
G. Accounting for Different Forms of Organization
The accounting mechanics, meaning double entry, adjustments, and statements, stay the same across organizational forms. What changes is mainly the equity section and the reporting emphasis, because the legal form changes who owns the entity and who is accountable to whom.
Sole proprietorship: one owner. Equity tracks capital, additional investment, profit or loss, and drawings. Drawings, meaning cash or goods the owner takes for personal use, reduce equity directly; they are not a business expense, because they are not incurred to earn revenue.
Partnership: two or more partners under an agreement. Each partner has a capital or current account, and profit or loss is split according to the agreed profit-sharing ratio, plus interest on capital or drawings or partner salary if the agreement provides for these. Example: partners A and B share profit 3 to 2; a distributable profit of Rs 100,000 splits into Rs 60,000 and Rs 40,000 before any other agreement-specific adjustments. The agreement, not a default assumption, governs every distribution detail.
Joint-stock company: a separate legal entity from its owners, with share capital, reserves, retained earnings, and a more formal reporting structure. Issuing shares for cash increases both cash and share capital. At this syllabus level, advanced company-accounting topics such as amalgamation, capital reduction, and consolidation of group accounts are explicitly outside scope.
Banking companies: a fundamentally different business model. Banks accept deposits, which are a major liability since the bank owes this money back to depositors, and extend financing, which is an asset, so their statements reflect a liquidity- and risk-driven structure rather than a typical trading firm’s inventory-and-sales structure.
Not-for-profit associations: formed to pursue a purpose, not to distribute profit. Their statements often use receipts-and-payments, a cash basis, or income-and-expenditure, an accrual basis, depending on what is required. Example: a membership subscription can count as income of the period it relates to even if the cash arrives at a different time, once accrual logic is applied.
Public-sector accounting: the accountability question shifts from did we earn a profit, to was public money used lawfully, transparently, and for its intended service purpose. The FPSC syllabus points toward the IPSAS-oriented framework used in Pakistan’s public sector as the reference point for this stewardship-centered reporting.
Key takeaway (Sections F and G): for any accounting-for-organizational-form question, first ask who is accountable to whom, and for what purpose does this entity exist. The accounting treatment follows from that, not the other way around.
H. Non-Current Tangible Assets and Depreciation
Non-current tangible assets are physical resources used for more than one accounting period, such as buildings or machinery. Key vocabulary: cost is what was paid to acquire and prepare the asset for use; residual value is the expected value at the end of useful life; depreciable amount is cost minus residual value, the amount that will be spread over the asset’s life; useful life is the period over which the asset is expected to be used.
A critical point: depreciation is an allocation of cost over time, not a cash payment. No money leaves the business when depreciation is recorded; it simply spreads an already-incurred cost across the periods that benefit from using the asset, matching expense to the revenue the asset helps generate.
Three common methods, using a machine costing Rs 500,000, with residual value Rs 50,000 and useful life 5 years, giving a depreciable amount of Rs 450,000:
Straight-line: depreciable amount divided by useful life, so 450,000 divided by 5 equals Rs 90,000 per year, every year, assuming assumptions don’t change. Simple and appropriate when the asset is used roughly evenly over time.
Reducing-balance: a fixed percentage is applied each year to the asset’s remaining book value, not the original cost, so depreciation is highest in early years and falls over time. This suits assets that lose most of their usefulness early, such as some vehicles and technology.
Units-of-production: depreciation is tied to actual usage, such as machine-hours or units produced, rather than time, so it varies with how intensively the asset is used in a given period. Most appropriate when wear is driven by use rather than the passage of time.
Choosing the wrong method distorts profit trends and asset values on the statement of financial position, which is exactly why the consistency concept from Section A applies directly here: switching depreciation methods without disclosure would make one year’s profit incomparable to another’s for reasons that have nothing to do with real performance.
I. Reading the Statements: Financial-Statement Analysis
Once statements exist, they need to be read, not just prepared.
Horizontal analysis, also called trend analysis, compares the same line item across multiple periods, such as sales in Year 1 versus Year 2 versus Year 3, to spot growth, decline, or volatility over time.
Vertical analysis expresses each line item as a percentage of a base figure within the same period, such as each expense as a percentage of sales. Ratio analysis goes further by relating two figures to each other: profitability ratios such as net profit margin, liquidity ratios such as the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), and solvency ratios such as debt-to-equity.
The consistency concept matters again here: ratios and trends are only meaningful if the underlying accounting methods haven’t silently changed between the periods being compared. Technical and industry analysis goes one step further by placing a company’s ratios in the context of its specific industry’s norms, since a good current ratio for a retailer and for a heavy manufacturer can look very different.
Paper I (Financial Accounting) key takeaways: the whole paper is one connected cycle, from transaction to journal to ledger to trial balance to adjustments to the four statements to closing entries to ratio analysis. Every foundational concept, such as accrual, matching, consistency, prudence, going concern, and substance over form, exists to prevent a specific kind of misleading information; learn the reason, not just the label. Double-entry direction depends on account type, not a universal rule. A balanced trial balance is a necessary but not sufficient check. Depreciation reallocates cost over time and is never a cash outflow. The organizational form mainly changes the equity treatment and the accountability lens, not the underlying mechanics. Ratios and trends are only trustworthy when accounting methods have been applied consistently across the periods being compared.

حدیث / صحیح روایت • مصدقہ عربی اقتباس؛ مطبوعہ ترجمے کا اقتباس

«مسلمان وہ ہے جس کی زبان اور ہاتھ سے مسلمان بچے رہیں»

ماخذ: صحیح بخاری، کتاب الایمان، حدیث 10؛ ترقیم: سنہ ڈاٹ کام۔ راوی: عبداللہ بن عمرو۔

ترجمہ: اسلامک اردو بکس پر موجود اردو ترجمے کا مسلسل اقتباس؛ متعلقہ اقتباس کے مترجم کی انفرادی نسبت کی تصدیق نہیں کی گئی۔

تعلق / سیاق: مسلمان ہونے کو ذمہ دار زبان اور عمل سے جوڑتی ہے۔ اس عبارت سے غیر مسلم کو نقصان کی اجازت نہیں نکلتی؛ آگے ممنوع اعمال چھوڑنے کو ہجرت کہا گیا ہے۔

حیثیت: صحیح: صحیح بخاری میں مروی؛ متن اور حوالہ جانچا گیا۔ یہ سند کی نئی مستقل تحقیق نہیں۔

موزوں استعمال: تعریف / استدلال

تصدیق: عربی / انگریزی · اردو

9
Din as sincerity and faithful concern
دین بطور اخلاص و خیر خواہی

الدِّينُ النَّصِيحَةُ

Hadith / authenticated report • Verified Arabic excerpt; published translation excerpt(s)

“The Religion is sincerity.”

Source: Sahih Muslim, Faith, hadith 55a; numbering: Sunnah.com. Narrator: Tamim al-Dari.

Translation: Established English wording displayed by Sunnah.com; individual translator not identified on the accessed passage.

Relevance / context: The explanation within the report names Allah, His Book, His Messenger, Muslim leaders and ordinary Muslims. Nasihah is therefore broader than merely offering occasional advice.

Status: Sahih: included in Sahih Muslim; text and locator checked. This is not a new independent isnad grading.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / English · Urdu

حدیث / صحیح روایت • مصدقہ عربی اقتباس؛ مطبوعہ ترجمے کا اقتباس

«دین خیر خواہی کا نام ہے»

ماخذ: صحیح مسلم، کتاب الایمان، حدیث 55a؛ ترقیم: سنہ ڈاٹ کام۔ راوی: تمیم داری۔

ترجمہ: ترجمہ شدہ احادیث نبویہ کا انسائیکلوپیڈیا (حدیث اِنک)، متعلقہ اردو حدیث کا متن یا عنوان؛ فردِ مترجم کی نسبت نہیں کی گئی۔

تعلق / سیاق: روایت کی اپنی وضاحت میں اللہ، اس کی کتاب، رسول، مسلمانوں کے قائدین اور عام مسلمان مذکور ہیں۔ نصیحت کا مفہوم اس لیے کبھی کبھار مشورہ دینے سے وسیع ہے۔

حیثیت: صحیح: صحیح مسلم میں مروی؛ متن اور حوالہ جانچا گیا۔ یہ سند کی نئی مستقل تحقیق نہیں۔

موزوں استعمال: تعریف / استدلال

10
Islam and iman in a particular Quranic context
ایک قرآنی سیاق میں اسلام اور ایمان

Tafsir • Scholarly position / paraphrased argument

Ibn Kathir reads iman here as more specific than outward Islam. He considers these Bedouins Muslims whose faith was not yet firmly established, rather than necessarily hypocrites; he records a different reading attributed to al-Bukhari.

Source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim; commentary on 49:14. King Saud University digital Quran project.

Relevance / context: Useful for distinguishing religious identity from inward conviction. The diagnosis is contextual, not a licence to judge unseen intentions.

Status: Cited passage inspected in the linked digital text. Attribution verified; interpretation is not classified as a Hadith. Print pagination not asserted.

Best use: Interpretation / critical analysis

Verify: Source passage

تفسیر • علمی مؤقف / مفہومی خلاصہ

ابن کثیر یہاں ایمان کو ظاہری اسلام سے خاص تر سمجھتے ہیں۔ ان کے نزدیک ان بدویوں کا ایمان ابھی پختہ نہیں ہوا تھا، مگر وہ لازماً منافق نہیں تھے۔ وہ امام بخاری سے منسوب مختلف تعبیر بھی ذکر کرتے ہیں۔

ماخذ: ابن کثیر، تفسیر القرآن العظیم؛ تفسیرِ آیت 49:14۔ جامعہ ملک سعود کا برقی قرآنی منصوبہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: دینی شناخت اور باطنی یقین کا فرق واضح ہوتا ہے۔ یہ سیاقی تعبیر ہے، پوشیدہ نیتوں کا فیصلہ کرنے کی اجازت نہیں۔

حیثیت: مربوط برقی متن میں مذکورہ مقام دیکھا گیا اور نسبت جانچی گئی۔ تفسیر یا علمی مؤقف کو حدیث کا درجہ نہیں دیا گیا۔ مطبوعہ صفحہ نمبر کا دعویٰ نہیں۔

موزوں استعمال: تعبیر / تنقیدی جائزہ

11
Submission and an integrated religious life
اطاعت اور مربوط دینی زندگی

Tafsir • Scholarly position / paraphrased argument

Maududi explains Islam in terms of recognising God as Lord, directing worship to Him, and following the guidance conveyed by His messengers. This is his interpretive account of the verse, not a separate Quranic translation.

Source: Sayyid Abul Ala Maududi, Tafhim al-Quran / Towards Understanding the Quran, commentary on 3:19, note 16; English text at IslamicStudies.info.

Relevance / context: Contributes an explicitly attributed modern exposition of the concept of Islam.

Status: Cited passage inspected in the linked digital text. Attribution verified; interpretation is not classified as a Hadith. Print pagination not asserted.

Best use: Interpretation / critical analysis

Verify: Source passage

تفسیر • علمی مؤقف / مفہومی خلاصہ

مودودی اسلام کی توضیح اللہ کو رب ماننے، اسی کی عبادت کرنے اور اس کے رسولوں کی لائی ہوئی ہدایت کی پیروی سے کرتے ہیں۔ یہ آیت کی ان کی تفسیری توضیح ہے، مستقل قرآنی ترجمہ نہیں۔

ماخذ: سید ابوالاعلیٰ مودودی، تفہیم القرآن / Towards Understanding the Quran، آیت 3:19، حاشیہ 16؛ معائنہ شدہ انگریزی متن: اسلامک اسٹڈیز ڈاٹ انفو۔

تعلق / سیاق: تصورِ اسلام کی واضح نسبت کے ساتھ جدید تفسیری توضیح فراہم کرتا ہے۔

حیثیت: مربوط برقی متن میں مذکورہ مقام دیکھا گیا اور نسبت جانچی گئی۔ تفسیر یا علمی مؤقف کو حدیث کا درجہ نہیں دیا گیا۔ مطبوعہ صفحہ نمبر کا دعویٰ نہیں۔

12
Worship includes inward and outward obedience
عبادت میں باطنی اور ظاہری اطاعت شامل ہے

العبادة هي اسم جامع لكل ما يحبه الله ويرضاه من الأقوال والأعمال الباطنة والظاهرة.

Classical or modern scholarship • Scholarly position / paraphrased argument

Ibn Taymiyyah includes approved inward and outward words and deeds within worship. His examples join ritual duties with honesty, trusts, family care, neighbourliness, patience and gratitude.

Source: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halim Ibn Taymiyyah, Al-Ubudiyyah, opening answer to the question “What is worship?”; Arabic digital transcription on Wikisource.

Relevance / context: The Arabic sentence is an exact scholarly quotation, not a Hadith. The bilingual explanations are paraphrases; the transcription was not collated with a print edition.

Status: Opening wording and attribution checked in the digital transcription; no claim of manuscript or critical-edition collation.

Best use: Interpretation / critical analysis

Verify: Source passage

قدیم یا جدید علمی مباحث • علمی مؤقف / مفہومی خلاصہ

ابن تیمیہ عبادت میں پسندیدہ باطنی و ظاہری اقوال اور اعمال کو شامل کرتے ہیں۔ ان کی مثالوں میں رسمی عبادات کے ساتھ سچائی، امانت، خاندان و ہمسایوں کی نگہداشت، صبر اور شکر بھی ہیں۔

ماخذ: احمد بن عبد الحلیم ابن تیمیہ، العبودیہ، سوال «عبادت کیا ہے؟» کا ابتدائی جواب؛ ویکی مصدر پر عربی برقی نقل۔

تعلق / سیاق: عربی جملہ عالم کے اصل الفاظ کا اقتباس ہے، حدیث نہیں۔ دو لسانی توضیحات مفہومی خلاصے ہیں؛ برقی نقل کا مطبوعہ نسخے سے مقابلہ نہیں کیا گیا۔

حیثیت: ابتدائی عبارت اور نسبت برقی نقل میں جانچی گئی؛ مخطوطے یا محقق مطبوعہ نسخے سے مقابلے کا دعویٰ نہیں۔

1
Islam as submission to God
اسلام: اللہ کے سامنے تسلیم و رضا

إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ اللَّهِ الْإِسْلَامُ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“Lo! religion with Allah (is) the Surrender (to His Will and Guidance).”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al Imran (3), ayah 19.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: The opening clause identifies Islam as the accepted din. The remainder concerns disagreement after knowledge; it is not reproduced here.

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«دین تو خدا کے نزدیک اسلام ہے»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ آل عمران (3)، آیت 19۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: ابتدائی فقرہ اسلام کو مقبول دین قرار دیتا ہے۔ باقی آیت علم کے بعد اختلاف کا ذکر کرتی ہے، جسے یہاں نقل نہیں کیا گیا۔

2
Theological claim of acceptance
دین کی قبولیت کا اعتقادی بیان

وَمَن يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ الْإِسْلَامِ دِينًا فَلَن يُقْبَلَ مِنْهُ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“And whoso seeketh as religion other than the Surrender (to Allah) it will not be accepted from him,”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al Imran (3), ayah 85.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: Records the Quranic claim about religious acceptance. It is a theological statement, not an instruction to coerce belief.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

«اور جو شخص اسلام کے سوا کسی اور دین کا طالب ہوگا وہ اس سے ہرگز قبول نہیں کیا جائے گا»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ آل عمران (3)، آیت 85۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: یہ دینی قبولیت کے متعلق قرآنی بیان ہے؛ کسی کو عقیدہ اختیار کرنے پر مجبور کرنے کا حکم نہیں۔

3
Abraham’s response of submission
ابراہیم علیہ السلام کا اقرارِ اطاعت

قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“he said: I have surrendered to the Lord of the Worlds.”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah (2), ayah 131.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: Gives a Quranic example of submission preceding the final Prophetic community; useful for Islam’s Abrahamic continuity.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«تو انہوں نے عرض کی کہ میں رب العالمین کے آگے سر اطاعت خم کرتا ہوں»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ البقرہ (2)، آیت 131۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: آخری امت سے پہلے اطاعت کی قرآنی مثال ہے؛ اسلام کے ابراہیمی تسلسل کی وضاحت میں مفید ہے۔

4
Submission joined to doing good
اطاعت کے ساتھ نیکوکاری

وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ دِينًا مِّمَّنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“Who is better in religion than he who surrendereth his purpose to Allah while doing good (to men)”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Nisa (4), ayah 125.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: Links surrender to moral excellence rather than a merely verbal religious identity. The verse continues with Abraham’s example.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«اور اس شخص سے کس کا دین اچھا ہوسکتا ہے جس نے حکم خدا کو قبول کیا اور وہ نیکوکار بھی ہے۔»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ النساء (4)، آیت 125۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: محض زبانی شناخت کے بجائے اطاعت کو نیکوکاری سے جوڑتی ہے۔ آگے آیت میں ابراہیم علیہ السلام کی مثال ہے۔

حیثیت: عربی اور نقل کردہ مطبوعہ تراجم کے الفاظ مربوط برقی متون سے جانچے گئے۔

5
Continuity of prophetic religion
انبیاء کے دین کا تسلسل

أَنْ أَقِيمُوا الدِّينَ وَلَا تَتَفَرَّقُوا فِيهِ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“Establish the religion, and be not divided therein.”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Shura (42), ayah 13.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: The surrounding passage names Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus. The command presents continuity and unity; detailed institutional applications require further argument.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«(وہ یہ) کہ دین کو قائم رکھنا اور اس میں پھوٹ نہ ڈالنا۔»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ الشوریٰ (42)، آیت 13۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: آیت کے سیاق میں نوح، ابراہیم، موسیٰ اور عیسیٰ علیہم السلام مذکور ہیں۔ حکم تسلسل اور وحدت بیان کرتا ہے؛ تفصیلی ادارہ جاتی اطلاق الگ استدلال چاہتا ہے۔

6
Outward submission and inward faith
ظاہری اسلام اور باطنی ایمان

وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“for the faith hath not yet entered into your hearts.”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Hujurat (49), ayah 14.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: In addressing these Bedouins, the verse distinguishes a claim of faith from submission. General theological relations between iman and Islam require the wider textual evidence.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«اور ایمان تو ہنوز تمہارے دلوں میں داخل ہی نہیں ہوا۔»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ الحجرات (49)، آیت 14۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: ان اعراب کے خطاب میں دعوائے ایمان اور اسلام کا فرق بیان ہوا ہے۔ ایمان و اسلام کے عمومی کلامی تعلق کے لیے دوسرے نصوص بھی درکار ہیں۔

Why Nations Fail Summary

by Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson

Why Nations Fail explains why some countries become wealthy, stable and technologically advanced while others remain poor, unequal and politically unstable. Why Nations Fail explains why some countries become wealthy, stable and technologically advanced while others remain poor, unequal and politically unstable. The authors argue that the main difference lies in institutions, meaning the rules and organizations that govern political and economic life. Inclusive institutions give ordinary people opportunities, legal protection, education and a voice in government. Extractive institutions concentrate wealth and power in the hands of a small ruling group. Geography, culture and natural resources may influence development, but political and economic institutions determine whether these advantages are used for the whole population or captured by elites.

Institutions determine national success: Countries generally prosper when their political and economic systems allow broad public participation.
Inclusive economic institutions create opportunity: People must be free to choose professions, establish businesses, own property and benefit from their work.
Inclusive political institutions distribute power: Political authority should not remain permanently in the hands of one family, military group, party or social class.
Extractive institutions benefit a small elite: Such institutions use taxation, corruption, forced labour, monopolies or political control to take resources from the majority.
Economic growth needs innovation: New technology and new businesses challenge older systems, but ruling elites may oppose innovation when it threatens their power.
Creative destruction is necessary: Progress replaces old industries, technologies and power structures with better ones, although those benefiting from the old system often resist change.
Natural wealth alone cannot guarantee prosperity: A country may possess oil, minerals or fertile land but remain poor if its resources are controlled by a narrow elite.
History creates institutional paths: Important events such as revolutions, wars, colonization and constitutional reforms can place countries on different paths.
Political reform and economic reform are connected: Lasting economic progress is difficult without accountable government, rule of law and protection of citizens’ rights.
Important quotation: “The most common reason why nations fail today is because they have extractive institutions.”

Why Nations Fail explains why some countries become wealthy, stable and technologically advanced while others remain poor, unequal and politically unstable. The authors argue that the main difference lies in institutions, meaning the rules and organizations that govern political and economic life. Inclusive institutions give ordinary people opportunities, legal protection, education and a voice in government. Extractive institutions concentrate wealth and power in the hands of a small ruling group. Geography, culture and natural resources may influence development, but political and economic institutions determine whether these advantages are used for the whole population or captured by elites.

Institutions determine national success: Countries generally prosper when their political and economic systems allow broad public participation.
Inclusive economic institutions create opportunity: People must be free to choose professions, establish businesses, own property and benefit from their work.
Inclusive political institutions distribute power: Political authority should not remain permanently in the hands of one family, military group, party or social class.
Extractive institutions benefit a small elite: Such institutions use taxation, corruption, forced labour, monopolies or political control to take resources from the majority.
Economic growth needs innovation: New technology and new businesses challenge older systems, but ruling elites may oppose innovation when it threatens their power.
Creative destruction is necessary: Progress replaces old industries, technologies and power structures with better ones, although those benefiting from the old system often resist change.
Natural wealth alone cannot guarantee prosperity: A country may possess oil, minerals or fertile land but remain poor if its resources are controlled by a narrow elite.
History creates institutional paths: Important events such as revolutions, wars, colonization and constitutional reforms can place countries on different paths.
Political reform and economic reform are connected: Lasting economic progress is difficult without accountable government, rule of law and protection of citizens’ rights.
Important quotation: “The most common reason why nations fail today is because they have extractive institutions.”

Paper I - Financial Accounting (50 Marks)

Accounting & Auditing · Group 1 · 2,504 words · about 13 min read

 On this page

A. The Ideas Behind the Rules (Accounting Concepts and Qualities)
B. The Accounting Equation and Double Entry
C. The Recording Cycle: Journal to Ledger to Trial Balance
D. Period-End Adjustments
E. The Four Financial Statements, and How They Connect
F. Who Reads This, and Why It Matters
G. Accounting for Different Forms of Organization
H. Non-Current Tangible Assets and Depreciation
I. Reading the Statements: Financial-Statement Analysis

Test paragraph only.

Treat this paper as one continuous story rather than 29 separate facts. A transaction happens; it is recorded through double entry; entries are grouped into ledger accounts; the ledger is checked through a trial balance; end-of-period adjustments correct timing issues; the corrected figures become four connected statements; and those statements are then read and compared through ratios. Everything below sits somewhere on that line.

A. The Ideas Behind the Rules (Accounting Concepts and Qualities)

Before any numbers, accounting rests on a small set of assumptions and qualities. Each one exists to stop financial statements from becoming misleading, and each shows up later as a reason why a specific rule works the way it does.

Accrual and matching: Income is recorded when it is earned, and expenses when they are incurred, not simply when cash changes hands. Matching then ties an expense to the period whose revenue it helped generate. Why it matters: without accrual accounting, a firm that delays paying its bills would look artificially profitable, and one that pays early would look artificially poor. Example: electricity used in June but paid in July is still June’s expense, because the use happened in June.
Consistency and comparability: The same accounting method should be used period after period unless there is a genuine, disclosed reason to change. This is what makes a trend meaningful rather than an artifact of switching methods.
True and fair presentation: The overall objective that statements should faithfully represent the entity’s actual financial reality, not just satisfy a checklist.
Neutrality, materiality, prudence, completeness, understandability: These are the qualities that make information useful. Neutral means not deliberately slanted. Material means important enough that its omission could change a user’s decision, and materiality is relative to the size of the entity. Prudence means exercising care under uncertainty; it is not permission to deliberately understate profit or assets. Completeness means nothing relevant has been left out. Understandability means a reasonably informed reader can follow the report.
Going concern and substance over form: Going concern assumes the business will keep operating for the foreseeable future, which justifies carrying assets at cost rather than forced-sale value. Substance over form means the economic reality of a transaction governs its accounting treatment, even if its legal label suggests otherwise.

Key takeaway: every one of these concepts answers the same question: what would make this information misleading, and how do we stop that? Learn them that way rather than as unconnected vocabulary.

B. The Accounting Equation and Double Entry

The entire system rests on one identity that must hold after every single transaction: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

Double entry is the mechanism that keeps this equation balanced: every transaction is recorded as at least one debit and one equal credit. A common beginner error is treating “debit” as meaning “increase” in general; it depends entirely on the account type:

Assets and expenses normally increase with a debit and decrease with a credit.
Liabilities, equity and income normally increase with a credit and decrease with a debit.

Worked example: the owner invests Rs 100,000 cash into the business. Cash (an asset) increases, so it is debited Rs 100,000. Capital (equity) increases, so it is credited Rs 100,000. The equation still balances.

The practical skill here is not memorizing rules but being able to ask, for any transaction: which two (or more) accounts changed, and in which direction? Working through many small transactions by hand, at least 30 as a starting target, is what turns this from a rule you look up into a reflex.

C. The Recording Cycle: Journal to Ledger to Trial Balance
General journal. Transactions are first recorded chronologically with a debit line, a credit line, and a short narration explaining what occurred. Example: a credit sale of Rs 20,000 is recorded as Debit Accounts Receivable 20,000, Credit Sales 20,000, because the business now has a right to collect cash later and has earned revenue now.
General ledger. The journal tells you what happened and when; the ledger reorganizes that same information by account, so you can ask what the balance of Cash is right now and get a single answer.
Trial balance. This lists every ledger account’s closing balance in two columns and checks that total debits equal total credits. It is a mechanical check, not a proof of correctness: some errors, such as omitting a transaction entirely, leave the trial balance perfectly balanced while the records are still wrong.
D. Period-End Adjustments
Before final statements can be prepared, the trial balance is adjusted to reflect the accrual concept properly. The four classic adjustments are:
Accrued expense: incurred but not yet paid or recorded, such as wages earned by staff in the last week of the period but paid next month.
Prepaid expense: paid in advance but not yet used up. A 12-month insurance premium of Rs 12,000 paid at the start of the year means that after 3 months, Rs 3,000 has been used and is an expense, and Rs 9,000 remains an asset called prepaid insurance.
Accrued income: earned but not yet received or recorded.
Unearned income: cash received, but the service or goods have not yet been delivered, so it is a liability until earned.
Once these are posted, an adjusted trial balance is produced, and this, not the original trial balance, is what final statements are built from.
A worksheet is an internal working paper used to organize the unadjusted balances, the adjustments, and the resulting adjusted figures side by side before the statements are typed up; it is a working tool, not a reported statement. Closing entries then transfer all temporary accounts, meaning revenue and expense accounts, into equity, because these accounts must start each new period at zero; permanent accounts simply carry their balances forward. Reversing entries, used optionally at the start of the next period, are a bookkeeping convenience that simplifies handling certain accruals.
Key takeaway (Sections B to D): the whole cycle is transaction, then journal, then ledger, then trial balance, then adjustments, then adjusted trial balance, then statements, then closing entries, then post-closing trial balance. If any stage feels abstract, carry one small transaction through the entire sequence by hand rather than memorizing each stage separately.
E. The Four Financial Statements, and How They Connect
A common mistake is treating profit, cash, and financial position as if they were the same thing. They are not, and each statement answers a different question.
Income statement: did we make a profit or loss over the period? Revenue minus expenses equals profit or loss. Example: revenue 500,000 minus expenses 420,000 gives profit 80,000.
Statement of financial position (balance sheet): what do we own and owe right now, at a single date? It lists assets (resources the entity controls), liabilities (present obligations it owes), and equity (the residual claim left after liabilities are deducted from assets), usually split into current and non-current items. Cash is normally current; a building used in operations is normally non-current.
Statement of cash flows: where did our cash actually come from and go, over the period? It explains cash movement under three headings: operating (day-to-day trading), investing (buying or selling long-term assets), and financing (borrowing, repaying, or raising capital). A firm can be profitable on paper while cash is tight, for example because customers haven’t paid yet, which is exactly why this statement exists alongside the income statement.
Statement of changes in equity: why did owners’ equity change over the period? It reconciles opening equity to closing equity by adding profit and any new owner contributions, and subtracting dividends or drawings and losses. Example: opening equity 1,000,000 plus profit 200,000 minus dividends 80,000 equals closing equity 1,120,000. This closing figure must always agree with the equity section of the statement of financial position, which is a good way to catch errors.
The connection to hold onto: profit from the income statement flows into equity via the statement of changes in equity, and the resulting equity balance appears on the statement of financial position, while the statement of cash flows tracks something related but genuinely different: cash movement, not profit.
F. Who Reads This, and Why It Matters
Different users read the same statements looking for different things.
External users: investors and shareholders look mainly at profitability and growth; lenders and banks look mainly at repayment capacity and cash flow; suppliers look mainly at short-term liquidity, meaning whether they will be paid on time; government and regulators look mainly at compliance and tax.
Internal users: directors and managers care about efficiency and decision-making; employees care about job security and stability.
A useful exam technique: build a user-to-information-need table for any organizational-form question, because it converts a vague theory prompt into a structured, markable answer.
G. Accounting for Different Forms of Organization
The accounting mechanics, meaning double entry, adjustments, and statements, stay the same across organizational forms. What changes is mainly the equity section and the reporting emphasis, because the legal form changes who owns the entity and who is accountable to whom.
Sole proprietorship: one owner. Equity tracks capital, additional investment, profit or loss, and drawings. Drawings, meaning cash or goods the owner takes for personal use, reduce equity directly; they are not a business expense, because they are not incurred to earn revenue.
Partnership: two or more partners under an agreement. Each partner has a capital or current account, and profit or loss is split according to the agreed profit-sharing ratio, plus interest on capital or drawings or partner salary if the agreement provides for these. Example: partners A and B share profit 3 to 2; a distributable profit of Rs 100,000 splits into Rs 60,000 and Rs 40,000 before any other agreement-specific adjustments. The agreement, not a default assumption, governs every distribution detail.
Joint-stock company: a separate legal entity from its owners, with share capital, reserves, retained earnings, and a more formal reporting structure. Issuing shares for cash increases both cash and share capital. At this syllabus level, advanced company-accounting topics such as amalgamation, capital reduction, and consolidation of group accounts are explicitly outside scope.
Banking companies: a fundamentally different business model. Banks accept deposits, which are a major liability since the bank owes this money back to depositors, and extend financing, which is an asset, so their statements reflect a liquidity- and risk-driven structure rather than a typical trading firm’s inventory-and-sales structure.
Not-for-profit associations: formed to pursue a purpose, not to distribute profit. Their statements often use receipts-and-payments, a cash basis, or income-and-expenditure, an accrual basis, depending on what is required. Example: a membership subscription can count as income of the period it relates to even if the cash arrives at a different time, once accrual logic is applied.
Public-sector accounting: the accountability question shifts from did we earn a profit, to was public money used lawfully, transparently, and for its intended service purpose. The FPSC syllabus points toward the IPSAS-oriented framework used in Pakistan’s public sector as the reference point for this stewardship-centered reporting.
Key takeaway (Sections F and G): for any accounting-for-organizational-form question, first ask who is accountable to whom, and for what purpose does this entity exist. The accounting treatment follows from that, not the other way around.
H. Non-Current Tangible Assets and Depreciation
Non-current tangible assets are physical resources used for more than one accounting period, such as buildings or machinery. Key vocabulary: cost is what was paid to acquire and prepare the asset for use; residual value is the expected value at the end of useful life; depreciable amount is cost minus residual value, the amount that will be spread over the asset’s life; useful life is the period over which the asset is expected to be used.
A critical point: depreciation is an allocation of cost over time, not a cash payment. No money leaves the business when depreciation is recorded; it simply spreads an already-incurred cost across the periods that benefit from using the asset, matching expense to the revenue the asset helps generate.
Three common methods, using a machine costing Rs 500,000, with residual value Rs 50,000 and useful life 5 years, giving a depreciable amount of Rs 450,000:
Straight-line: depreciable amount divided by useful life, so 450,000 divided by 5 equals Rs 90,000 per year, every year, assuming assumptions don’t change. Simple and appropriate when the asset is used roughly evenly over time.
Reducing-balance: a fixed percentage is applied each year to the asset’s remaining book value, not the original cost, so depreciation is highest in early years and falls over time. This suits assets that lose most of their usefulness early, such as some vehicles and technology.
Units-of-production: depreciation is tied to actual usage, such as machine-hours or units produced, rather than time, so it varies with how intensively the asset is used in a given period. Most appropriate when wear is driven by use rather than the passage of time.
Choosing the wrong method distorts profit trends and asset values on the statement of financial position, which is exactly why the consistency concept from Section A applies directly here: switching depreciation methods without disclosure would make one year’s profit incomparable to another’s for reasons that have nothing to do with real performance.
I. Reading the Statements: Financial-Statement Analysis
Once statements exist, they need to be read, not just prepared.
Horizontal analysis, also called trend analysis, compares the same line item across multiple periods, such as sales in Year 1 versus Year 2 versus Year 3, to spot growth, decline, or volatility over time.
Vertical analysis expresses each line item as a percentage of a base figure within the same period, such as each expense as a percentage of sales. Ratio analysis goes further by relating two figures to each other: profitability ratios such as net profit margin, liquidity ratios such as the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), and solvency ratios such as debt-to-equity.
The consistency concept matters again here: ratios and trends are only meaningful if the underlying accounting methods haven’t silently changed between the periods being compared. Technical and industry analysis goes one step further by placing a company’s ratios in the context of its specific industry’s norms, since a good current ratio for a retailer and for a heavy manufacturer can look very different.
Paper I (Financial Accounting) key takeaways: the whole paper is one connected cycle, from transaction to journal to ledger to trial balance to adjustments to the four statements to closing entries to ratio analysis. Every foundational concept, such as accrual, matching, consistency, prudence, going concern, and substance over form, exists to prevent a specific kind of misleading information; learn the reason, not just the label. Double-entry direction depends on account type, not a universal rule. A balanced trial balance is a necessary but not sufficient check. Depreciation reallocates cost over time and is never a cash outflow. The organizational form mainly changes the equity treatment and the accountability lens, not the underlying mechanics. Ratios and trends are only trustworthy when accounting methods have been applied consistently across the periods being compared.

Choosing the wrong method distorts profit trends and asset values on the statement of financial position, which is exactly why the consistency concept from Section A applies directly here: switching depreciation methods without disclosure would make one year’s profit incomparable to another’s for reasons that have nothing to do with real performance.
I. Reading the Statements: Financial-Statement Analysis
Once statements exist, they need to be read, not just prepared.
Horizontal analysis, also called trend analysis, compares the same line item across multiple periods, such as sales in Year 1 versus Year 2 versus Year 3, to spot growth, decline, or volatility over time.
Vertical analysis expresses each line item as a percentage of a base figure within the same period, such as each expense as a percentage of sales. Ratio analysis goes further by relating two figures to each other: profitability ratios such as net profit margin, liquidity ratios such as the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), and solvency ratios such as debt-to-equity.
The consistency concept matters again here: ratios and trends are only meaningful if the underlying accounting methods haven’t silently changed between the periods being compared. Technical and industry analysis goes one step further by placing a company’s ratios in the context of its specific industry’s norms, since a good current ratio for a retailer and for a heavy manufacturer can look very different.
Paper I (Financial Accounting) key takeaways: the whole paper is one connected cycle, from transaction to journal to ledger to trial balance to adjustments to the four statements to closing entries to ratio analysis. Every foundational concept, such as accrual, matching, consistency, prudence, going concern, and substance over form, exists to prevent a specific kind of misleading information; learn the reason, not just the label. Double-entry direction depends on account type, not a universal rule. A balanced trial balance is a necessary but not sufficient check. Depreciation reallocates cost over time and is never a cash outflow. The organizational form mainly changes the equity treatment and the accountability lens, not the underlying mechanics. Ratios and trends are only trustworthy when accounting methods have been applied consistently across the periods being compared.

1
Islam as submission to God
اسلام: اللہ کے سامنے تسلیم و رضا

إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ اللَّهِ الْإِسْلَامُ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“Lo! religion with Allah (is) the Surrender (to His Will and Guidance).”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al Imran (3), ayah 19.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: The opening clause identifies Islam as the accepted din. The remainder concerns disagreement after knowledge; it is not reproduced here.

«دین تو خدا کے نزدیک اسلام ہے»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ آل عمران (3)، آیت 19۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: ابتدائی فقرہ اسلام کو مقبول دین قرار دیتا ہے۔ باقی آیت علم کے بعد اختلاف کا ذکر کرتی ہے، جسے یہاں نقل نہیں کیا گیا۔

حیثیت: عربی اور نقل کردہ مطبوعہ تراجم کے الفاظ مربوط برقی متون سے جانچے گئے۔

2
Theological claim of acceptance
دین کی قبولیت کا اعتقادی بیان

وَمَن يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ الْإِسْلَامِ دِينًا فَلَن يُقْبَلَ مِنْهُ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“And whoso seeketh as religion other than the Surrender (to Allah) it will not be accepted from him,”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al Imran (3), ayah 85.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: Records the Quranic claim about religious acceptance. It is a theological statement, not an instruction to coerce belief.

«اور جو شخص اسلام کے سوا کسی اور دین کا طالب ہوگا وہ اس سے ہرگز قبول نہیں کیا جائے گا»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ آل عمران (3)، آیت 85۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

3
Abraham’s response of submission
ابراہیم علیہ السلام کا اقرارِ اطاعت

قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“he said: I have surrendered to the Lord of the Worlds.”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah (2), ayah 131.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: Gives a Quranic example of submission preceding the final Prophetic community; useful for Islam’s Abrahamic continuity.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«تو انہوں نے عرض کی کہ میں رب العالمین کے آگے سر اطاعت خم کرتا ہوں»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ البقرہ (2)، آیت 131۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: آخری امت سے پہلے اطاعت کی قرآنی مثال ہے؛ اسلام کے ابراہیمی تسلسل کی وضاحت میں مفید ہے۔

4
Submission joined to doing good
اطاعت کے ساتھ نیکوکاری

وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ دِينًا مِّمَّنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“Who is better in religion than he who surrendereth his purpose to Allah while doing good (to men)”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Nisa (4), ayah 125.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: Links surrender to moral excellence rather than a merely verbal religious identity. The verse continues with Abraham’s example.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«اور اس شخص سے کس کا دین اچھا ہوسکتا ہے جس نے حکم خدا کو قبول کیا اور وہ نیکوکار بھی ہے۔»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ النساء (4)، آیت 125۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: محض زبانی شناخت کے بجائے اطاعت کو نیکوکاری سے جوڑتی ہے۔ آگے آیت میں ابراہیم علیہ السلام کی مثال ہے۔

حیثیت: عربی اور نقل کردہ مطبوعہ تراجم کے الفاظ مربوط برقی متون سے جانچے گئے۔

5
Continuity of prophetic religion
انبیاء کے دین کا تسلسل

أَنْ أَقِيمُوا الدِّينَ وَلَا تَتَفَرَّقُوا فِيهِ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“Establish the religion, and be not divided therein.”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Shura (42), ayah 13.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: The surrounding passage names Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus. The command presents continuity and unity; detailed institutional applications require further argument.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / Urdu · English

قرآنی شواہد • آیت کا مسلسل اقتباس

«(وہ یہ) کہ دین کو قائم رکھنا اور اس میں پھوٹ نہ ڈالنا۔»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ الشوریٰ (42)، آیت 13۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: آیت کے سیاق میں نوح، ابراہیم، موسیٰ اور عیسیٰ علیہم السلام مذکور ہیں۔ حکم تسلسل اور وحدت بیان کرتا ہے؛ تفصیلی ادارہ جاتی اطلاق الگ استدلال چاہتا ہے۔

Outward submission and inward faith
ظاہری اسلام اور باطنی ایمان

وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ

Qur’anic evidence • Contiguous ayah excerpt

“for the faith hath not yet entered into your hearts.”

Source: Qur'an, Surah Al-Hujurat (49), ayah 14.

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran; accessed through Quranic Arabic Corpus.

Relevance / context: In addressing these Bedouins, the verse distinguishes a claim of faith from submission. General theological relations between iman and Islam require the wider textual evidence.

Status: Arabic and the reproduced published translation wording checked in the linked digital texts.

«اور ایمان تو ہنوز تمہارے دلوں میں داخل ہی نہیں ہوا۔»

ماخذ: قرآن مجید، سورۃ الحجرات (49)، آیت 14۔

ترجمہ: فتح محمد جالندھری، ترجمۂ قرآن؛ رسائی: سورہ قرآن ویب گاہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: ان اعراب کے خطاب میں دعوائے ایمان اور اسلام کا فرق بیان ہوا ہے۔ ایمان و اسلام کے عمومی کلامی تعلق کے لیے دوسرے نصوص بھی درکار ہیں۔

7
Islam, faith and ihsan in the Hadith of Gabriel
حدیثِ جبریل میں اسلام، ایمان اور احسان

أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ

Hadith / authenticated report • Verified Arabic excerpt; published translation excerpt(s)

“That you worship Allah as if you are seeing Him, for though you don't see Him, He, verily, sees you.”

Source: Sahih Muslim, The Book of Faith, hadith 8a; numbering: Sunnah.com. Narrator: Umar ibn al-Khattab.

Translation: Established English wording displayed by Sunnah.com; individual translator not identified on the accessed passage.

Relevance / context: The complete report distinguishes Islam’s acts, faith in Allah, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day and decree, and ihsan. The excerpt concerns ihsan; the episode is identified as teaching din.

Status: Sahih: included in Sahih Muslim; text and locator checked. This is not a new independent isnad grading. Urdu translation not verified.

Best use: Definition / argument

Verify: Arabic / English

حدیث / صحیح روایت • مصدقہ عربی اقتباس؛ مطبوعہ ترجمے کا اقتباس

اس اندراج کے لیے کسی مطبوعہ اردو ترجمے کے الفاظ کی تصدیق نہیں ہو سکی؛ خودساختہ ترجمہ شامل نہیں کیا گیا۔

ماخذ: صحیح مسلم، کتاب الایمان، حدیث 8a؛ ترقیم: سنہ ڈاٹ کام۔ راوی: عمر بن خطاب۔

ترجمہ: مطبوعہ اردو ترجمہ: غیر مصدقہ / دستیاب اقتباس نقل نہیں کیا گیا۔

تعلق / سیاق: پوری روایت میں اسلام کے اعمال، اللہ، فرشتوں، کتابوں، رسولوں، آخرت اور تقدیر پر ایمان، اور احسان الگ بیان ہوتے ہیں۔ اقتباس احسان کے متعلق ہے؛ واقعے کو دین کی تعلیم کہا گیا ہے۔

حیثیت: صحیح: صحیح مسلم میں مروی؛ متن اور حوالہ جانچا گیا۔ یہ سند کی نئی مستقل تحقیق نہیں۔ اردو ترجمہ غیر مصدقہ ہے۔

8
Religious identity and freedom from harm
دینی شناخت اور ضرر سے حفاظت

الْمُسْلِمُ مَنْ سَلِمَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ وَيَدِهِ

Hadith / authenticated report • Verified Arabic excerpt; published translation excerpt(s)

“A Muslim is the one who avoids harming Muslims with his tongue and hands.”

Source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Belief, hadith 10; numbering: Sunnah.com. Narrator: Abdullah ibn Amr.

Translation: Established English wording displayed by Sunnah.com; individual translator not identified on the accessed passage.

Relevance / context: Connects being Muslim with accountable speech and action. The wording does not itself license harm to non-Muslims; the continuation describes abandoning prohibited acts as migration.

Status: Sahih: included in Sahih al-Bukhari; text and locator checked. This is not a new independent isnad grading.

Best use: Definition / argument

«مسلمان وہ ہے جس کی زبان اور ہاتھ سے مسلمان بچے رہیں»

ماخذ: صحیح بخاری، کتاب الایمان، حدیث 10؛ ترقیم: سنہ ڈاٹ کام۔ راوی: عبداللہ بن عمرو۔

ترجمہ: اسلامک اردو بکس پر موجود اردو ترجمے کا مسلسل اقتباس؛ متعلقہ اقتباس کے مترجم کی انفرادی نسبت کی تصدیق نہیں کی گئی۔

تعلق / سیاق: مسلمان ہونے کو ذمہ دار زبان اور عمل سے جوڑتی ہے۔ اس عبارت سے غیر مسلم کو نقصان کی اجازت نہیں نکلتی؛ آگے ممنوع اعمال چھوڑنے کو ہجرت کہا گیا ہے۔

حیثیت: صحیح: صحیح بخاری میں مروی؛ متن اور حوالہ جانچا گیا۔ یہ سند کی نئی مستقل تحقیق نہیں۔

9
Din as sincerity and faithful concern
دین بطور اخلاص و خیر خواہی

الدِّينُ النَّصِيحَةُ

Hadith / authenticated report • Verified Arabic excerpt; published translation excerpt(s)

“The Religion is sincerity.”

Source: Sahih Muslim, Faith, hadith 55a; numbering: Sunnah.com. Narrator: Tamim al-Dari.

«دین خیر خواہی کا نام ہے»

ماخذ: صحیح مسلم، کتاب الایمان، حدیث 55a؛ ترقیم: سنہ ڈاٹ کام۔ راوی: تمیم داری۔

ترجمہ: ترجمہ شدہ احادیث نبویہ کا انسائیکلوپیڈیا (حدیث اِنک)، متعلقہ اردو حدیث کا متن یا عنوان؛ فردِ مترجم کی نسبت نہیں کی گئی۔

10
Islam and iman in a particular Quranic context
ایک قرآنی سیاق میں اسلام اور ایمان

Tafsir • Scholarly position / paraphrased argument

Ibn Kathir reads iman here as more specific than outward Islam. He considers these Bedouins Muslims whose faith was not yet firmly established, rather than necessarily hypocrites; he records a different reading attributed to al-Bukhari.

Source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim; commentary on 49:14. King Saud University digital Quran project.

Relevance / context: Useful for distinguishing religious identity from inward conviction. The diagnosis is contextual, not a licence to judge unseen intentions.

تفسیر • علمی مؤقف / مفہومی خلاصہ

ابن کثیر یہاں ایمان کو ظاہری اسلام سے خاص تر سمجھتے ہیں۔ ان کے نزدیک ان بدویوں کا ایمان ابھی پختہ نہیں ہوا تھا، مگر وہ لازماً منافق نہیں تھے۔ وہ امام بخاری سے منسوب مختلف تعبیر بھی ذکر کرتے ہیں۔

ماخذ: ابن کثیر، تفسیر القرآن العظیم؛ تفسیرِ آیت 49:14۔ جامعہ ملک سعود کا برقی قرآنی منصوبہ۔

تعلق / سیاق: دینی شناخت اور باطنی یقین کا فرق واضح ہوتا ہے۔ یہ سیاقی تعبیر ہے، پوشیدہ نیتوں کا فیصلہ کرنے کی اجازت نہیں۔

حیثیت: مربوط برقی متن میں مذکورہ مقام دیکھا گیا اور نسبت جانچی گئی۔ تفسیر یا علمی مؤقف کو حدیث کا درجہ نہیں دیا گیا۔ مطبوعہ صفحہ نمبر کا دعویٰ نہیں۔

موزوں استعمال: تعبیر / تنقیدی جائزہ

تصدیق: اصل ماخذی مقام

11
Submission and an integrated religious life
اطاعت اور مربوط دینی زندگی

Tafsir • Scholarly position / paraphrased argument

Maududi explains Islam in terms of recognising God as Lord, directing worship to Him, and following the guidance conveyed by His messengers. This is his interpretive account of the verse, not a separate Quranic translation.

Source: Sayyid Abul Ala Maududi, Tafhim al-Quran / Towards Understanding the Quran, commentary on 3:19, note 16; English text at IslamicStudies.info.

Relevance / context: Contributes an explicitly attributed modern exposition of the concept of Islam.

Status: Cited passage inspected in the linked digital text. Attribution verified; interpretation is not classified as a Hadith. Print pagination not asserted.

Best use: Interpretation / critical analysis

Verify: Source passage

تفسیر • علمی مؤقف / مفہومی خلاصہ

مودودی اسلام کی توضیح اللہ کو رب ماننے، اسی کی عبادت کرنے اور اس کے رسولوں کی لائی ہوئی ہدایت کی پیروی سے کرتے ہیں۔ یہ آیت کی ان کی تفسیری توضیح ہے، مستقل قرآنی ترجمہ نہیں۔

ماخذ: سید ابوالاعلیٰ مودودی، تفہیم القرآن / Towards Understanding the Quran، آیت 3:19، حاشیہ 16؛ معائنہ شدہ انگریزی متن: اسلامک اسٹڈیز ڈاٹ انفو۔

تعلق / سیاق: تصورِ اسلام کی واضح نسبت کے ساتھ جدید تفسیری توضیح فراہم کرتا ہے۔

حیثیت: مربوط برقی متن میں مذکورہ مقام دیکھا گیا اور نسبت جانچی گئی۔ تفسیر یا علمی مؤقف کو حدیث کا درجہ نہیں دیا گیا۔ مطبوعہ صفحہ نمبر کا دعویٰ نہیں۔

موزوں استعمال: تعبیر / تنقیدی جائزہ

12
Worship includes inward and outward obedience
عبادت میں باطنی اور ظاہری اطاعت شامل ہے

العبادة هي اسم جامع لكل ما يحبه الله ويرضاه من الأقوال والأعمال الباطنة والظاهرة.

Classical or modern scholarship • Scholarly position / paraphrased argument

Ibn Taymiyyah includes approved inward and outward words and deeds within worship. His examples join ritual duties with honesty, trusts, family care, neighbourliness, patience and gratitude.

Source: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halim Ibn Taymiyyah, Al-Ubudiyyah, opening answer to the question “What is worship?”; Arabic digital transcription on Wikisource.

Relevance / context: The Arabic sentence is an exact scholarly quotation, not a Hadith. The bilingual explanations are paraphrases; the transcription was not collated with a print edition.

Status: Opening wording and attribution checked in the digital transcription; no claim of manuscript or critical-edition collation.

Best use: Interpretation / critical analysis

Verify: Source passage

قدیم یا جدید علمی مباحث • علمی مؤقف / مفہومی خلاصہ

ابن تیمیہ عبادت میں پسندیدہ باطنی و ظاہری اقوال اور اعمال کو شامل کرتے ہیں۔ ان کی مثالوں میں رسمی عبادات کے ساتھ سچائی، امانت، خاندان و ہمسایوں کی نگہداشت، صبر اور شکر بھی ہیں۔

ماخذ: احمد بن عبد الحلیم ابن تیمیہ، العبودیہ، سوال «عبادت کیا ہے؟» کا ابتدائی جواب؛ ویکی مصدر پر عربی برقی نقل۔

تعلق / سیاق: عربی جملہ عالم کے اصل الفاظ کا اقتباس ہے، حدیث نہیں۔ دو لسانی توضیحات مفہومی خلاصے ہیں؛ برقی نقل کا مطبوعہ نسخے سے مقابلہ نہیں کیا گیا۔

حیثیت: ابتدائی عبارت اور نسبت برقی نقل میں جانچی گئی؛ مخطوطے یا محقق مطبوعہ نسخے سے مقابلے کا دعویٰ نہیں۔
